q.t: Naturally occurring magnets are called…
q.e: Lodestones were used by early sailors.

q.t: Which is a magnetic material?
q.e: Iron, nickel and cobalt are magnetic.

q.t: Which metal is NOT magnetic?
q.e: Not every metal is magnetic — copper, aluminium, gold, silver are not.

q.t: Where on a bar magnet do most iron filings stick?
q.e: Attraction is strongest at the poles.

q.t: A freely suspended magnet comes to rest…
q.e: The Earth behaves like a giant magnet.

q.t: Like poles…
q.e: N–N or S–S push apart.

q.t: Unlike poles…
q.e: N–S pull together.

q.t: A magnetic compass contains a…
q.e: The needle settles north–south over a direction dial.

q.t: The north-pointing end of a compass needle is usually painted…
q.e: Red marks the north end.

q.t: Which is a common magnet shape?
q.e: Bar, U-shaped and ring magnets are common.

q.t: A bar magnet is broken in two. Each piece has…
o: Both a North and a South pole
q.e: A single pole can't exist; poles always come in pairs.

q.t: Why does a suspended magnet point north–south?
o: The Earth behaves like a giant magnet
q.e: The magnet lines up with the Earth's magnetism.

q.t: An iron bar is suspended. It comes to rest…
q.e: Only a magnet settles north–south.

q.t: What is the sure test for a magnet?
q.e: Iron is attracted by both poles; only a magnet can be repelled.

q.t: If two objects repel each other…
q.e: Only magnets push each other away (like poles).

q.t: A magnet attracts a compass needle through a sheet of cardboard. This shows…
o: Magnetic effect acts through non-magnetic materials
q.e: Wood, cardboard, plastic and glass don't block the effect.

q.t: To make a magnet from a needle, stroke it…
o: 30–40 times with one pole, in the same direction
q.e: Always the same pole, same direction, lifting at the end.

q.t: The matsya-yantra was…
o: A magnetised fish-shaped iron floating in oil
q.e: An ancient Indian navigation compass.

q.t: Bring a magnet's North pole near a compass's North end. The needle…
q.e: Like poles repel.

q.t: Why does a fridge magnet hold paper on the fridge?
o: Its effect passes through the paper to the iron door
q.e: Magnetic effect acts through non-magnetic paper.

q.t: You have a plain iron bar and a magnet that look alike. How can you tell which is which using only them?
o: Touch one's end to the other's middle — a magnet's end attracts strongly
q.e: A magnet's pole pulls on the iron's middle; the iron's end barely pulls the magnet's middle, where attraction is weakest.

q.t: Why can't attraction alone prove an object is a magnet?
o: A magnet attracts plain iron too
q.e: Iron is attracted by both poles.

q.t: A ring magnet is cut into 4 pieces. How many poles in total?
q.e: Each piece has a North and a South pole: 4 × 2 = 8.

q.t: How do you set a compass to read directions?
o: Rotate the box until N on the dial lines up with the needle
q.e: Then all directions read correctly off the dial.

q.t: Why should a compass be kept away from magnets?
o: The magnet would pull the needle off north
q.e: A nearby magnet's effect is stronger than the Earth's, giving wrong directions.

q.t: How do you test whether your stroked needle became a magnet?
o: See if it picks up pins or iron filings
q.e: A magnetised needle attracts small iron objects.

q.t: Why float the magnetised needle on a cork in water?
o: So it can turn freely to point north–south
q.e: Floating lets it rotate freely, like a suspended magnet.

q.t: Which list is all magnetic?
q.e: Iron, nickel and cobalt (and some mixtures) are magnetic.

q.t: Which pair would attract?
q.e: Unlike poles attract.

q.t: Ancient sailors used lodestones to…
q.e: A suspended lodestone points north–south.

q.t: Three bars A, B, C. A repels B. A attracts C. C attracts B. What can you conclude?
o: A and B are magnets; C may be plain iron
All three are magnets for sure
q.e: Repulsion proves A and B are magnets. Attraction alone can't prove C is a magnet.

q.t: A magnet's North pole repels end X of a bar. End X is…
q.e: Only like poles repel.

q.t: Placing a glass sheet between a magnet and a compass changes the needle's deflection…
q.e: Glass is non-magnetic; the effect passes through.

q.t: A gold ring is not pulled by a magnet. Why?
o: Gold is not a magnetic material
q.e: Being a metal doesn't make something magnetic.

q.t: In the needle-making method, why lift the magnet at the end of each stroke?
o: So every stroke goes the same direction
q.e: Stroking back would undo the alignment.

q.t: The end of a suspended magnet that points north is called…
q.e: It seeks north, so it's called the North pole.

q.t: A magnetic pencil box stays shut through its plastic lid. Why?
o: The magnetic effect passes through plastic
q.e: Non-magnetic materials don't block magnetism.

q.t: Can you get a magnet with only a North pole by cutting it very small?
o: No — every piece has both poles
q.e: However small, both poles appear.

q.t: Which object would a magnet NOT pick up?
q.e: Copper is non-magnetic.

q.t: Bring a magnet's South pole near a compass's North end. The needle…
q.e: Unlike poles attract.
